problem: VLN agents generalize poorly to unseen scenes because human-annotated data (R2R: 22k instructions, 61 MP3D training scans) is scarce. Prior HM3D/Gibson-based augmentation has its own flaws. AutoVLN's graphs are sparse and 29% of their edges cross obstacles. MARVAL depends on non-public models (Marky speaker, MURAL encoder) and a learned navigability predictor. Neither work studies which parts of the data pipeline or which training recipe actually matter.
motivation: More diverse traversable environments and more in-domain instruction-trajectory supervision are known to improve generalization. Building such data, however, requires several sub-steps that each affect data quality: graph construction, fixing corrupted mesh renders, and instruction generation. How to use large augmented data in pre-training versus fine-tuning had also not been studied. The authors want a fully reproducible, public-resource pipeline and a component-wise analysis that can serve as a guideline.
key_idea: Build dense, fully-traversable navigation graphs on 1,291 HM3D and Gibson scans. Repair the faulty mesh renders with a Co-Mod GAN trained on MP3D rendered/camera image pairs. Label about 4.9M sampled shortest paths with the off-the-shelf EnvDrop speaker. Use this ScaleVLN data in both pre-training (MLM+SAP) and DAgger fine-tuning of existing agents (DUET, HAMT).
insight: Data quality and diversity matter more than raw quantity. (1) Graph quality: AutoVLN graphs (29.35% colliding edges) give no gain on val-unseen R2R (72.75 SR vs 72.92 without HM3D data), while ScaleVLN's collision-free dense graphs give 76.01. (2) Scene diversity beats sample count: at a fixed 700k samples, 200/400/800 scenes give 74.84/75.22/76.25 SR, whereas raising samples from 700k to 2890k on 800 scenes only reaches 76.59. (3) Image repair: it matters most for low-quality Gibson meshes; adding unrepaired Gibson data is worse (76.33) than repaired Gibson (78.08). (4) Training recipe: keeping HM3D augmented data in fine-tuning adds +2.51 SR (79.10) and shrinks the seen/unseen gap to under 1%, while adding PREVALENT to fine-tuning hurts (77.10) through overfitting to the 61 MP3D scans. MLM+SAP is the best pre-training combination; adding MRM slightly hurts (75.82). Once data is scaled, depth input stops helping, a cheap LSTM speaker beats fine-tuned GPT-2, and the remaining ~6% gap to humans matches the OSR–SR gap, which points to stopping as the next bottleneck.
method: Environment collection: 800 HM3D train scenes plus 491 Gibson train/val scenes, over 150k m² navigable area, about 7.5× the MP3D training area.

Navigation-graph construction: (1) over-sample navigable points with Habitat, keeping pairwise geodesic distance > 0.4 m; (2) merge them by Agglomerative Clustering with a 1.0 m threshold so nodes sit near open-space centers; (3) connect nodes randomly within 5.0 m, capped at 5 edges per node; (4) refine with the graph-refinement method of Hong et al. 2022 into fully-connected, fully-traversable graphs. Result: average edge 1.41 m, average degree 4.55, 0% colliding edges.

Faulty-render recovery: a Co-Modulated GAN, trained as image-to-image translation on MP3D rendered/camera image pairs, repairs broken, distorted or missing regions. It is applied to four overlapping 512×512 crops of each 512×1024 panorama, from which the 36 discrete views are extracted.

Trajectory sampling: following PREVALENT, all shortest paths between node pairs with 3–5 intermediate nodes are collected, giving 2,890,267 HM3D and 2,051,443 Gibson paths. For REVERIE-style data, paths of 4–9 edges end at viewpoints with visible objects within 3 m (518,233 HM3D + 311,976 Gibson).

Instruction generation: the off-the-shelf LSTM EnvDrop speaker trained on R2R labels the R2R-style data, 4,941,710 pairs in total (352× R2R, 4.62× PREVALENT). REVERIE data (830,209 pairs) uses a GPT-2 speaker prompted only with the target object.

Agent training: DUET (R2R/CVDN/REVERIE) or HAMT (R2R-CE, with a candidate waypoint predictor) over CLIP ViT-B/16 features, with the LXMERT-initialized language and cross-modal encoder. Pre-training uses MLM+SAP on R2R + PREVALENT + ScaleVLN (plus Object Grounding for REVERIE). Fine-tuning uses DAgger-style imitation learning on R2R + HM-E; Gibson and PREVALENT data are excluded from fine-tuning.

numbers_note: The R2R main table gives the headline methods only as integers (e.g. SR 79/80); the ablation tables give two-decimal values for intermediate configurations, such as Method #6 at 79.10 SR val-unseen. In the R4R table CLS is printed with a ↓ arrow although higher is better, and values are copied as printed. The text says ScaleVLN gives Seq2Seq a 12.2% SR gain, which does not match the table (37.34→47.51).
results:
On R2R test-unseen, DUET+ScaleVLN reaches SR 77 / SPL 68. With CLIP ViT-H/14 and EnvEdit it reaches SR 80 / SPL 70 in a single run, against the previous best BEVBert at 73/62 and human performance at 86/76. It ranked first on the leaderboard, ahead of beam-search and pre-exploration entries, and the seen/unseen gap closes to under 1%. The same data sets new state of the art on the other benchmarks:
- REVERIE test: SR 56.13 / SPL 39.52, versus AutoVLN at 55.17 / 38.88.
- CVDN test: GP 6.97, versus HAMT at 5.58.
- R2R-CE test: SR 55 / SPL 50, versus Ego²-Map at 47 / 41.
limitations: The EnvDrop and GPT-2 speakers produce low-quality instructions (Bleu-4 27.66 / 24.36); the authors identify better instruction generation as future work.

The data is discrete (nav-graph) and Gibson-derived data is too far from MP3D to help fine-tuning. R2R-CE still relies on a waypoint predictor, and the agents assume panoramic observations, unlike egocentric human followers.

A remaining gap to humans of about 6% SR matches the OSR–SR gap, so stopping decisions remain unsolved. Gains from more samples per scene saturate: 700k→2890k samples on 800 scenes gives only about +0.3 SR.
